nameStory: The milky slug gets its common name from the thick, milky-white mucus it produces when disturbed or threatened. This creamy slime is much more noticeable than the clear trail most slugs leave behind, making it look like someone spilled milk in the garden. The scientific name 'reticulatum' refers to the net-like pattern often visible on its skin.
description: The milky slug is a small, soft-bodied land mollusk that moves by gliding on a trail of slime. These garden visitors are typically gray or brownish in color and reach about 1-2 inches long when fully extended. Like all slugs, they're basically snails without shells, with two pairs of tentacles on their heads - the longer pair has eyes at the tips. They're considered an important agricultural pest because they love to munch on crops and garden plants.

idTips.label: Milky mucus
idTips.description: When touched or startled, produces thick, white or cream-colored slime that's much more opaque than other slugs' clear trails

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Small and elongated, about 1-2 inches when extended, with a relatively slender body compared to larger garden slugs

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: Typically gray to light brown with darker mottling or a faint net-like pattern visible on the skin, especially when moist

idTips.label: Breathing pore
idTips.description: Has a small, round breathing hole (pneumostome) on the right side of its body, about halfway back from the head

idTips.label: Tentacles
idTips.description: Four tentacles on the head - two long ones with dark eye spots at the tips, and two shorter ones below for smell and taste

habitat: Milky slugs thrive in moist environments throughout New England, especially in gardens, agricultural fields, and disturbed areas with rich soil. They're commonly found hiding under logs, rocks, mulch, or in compost piles during the day. You'll also spot them in meadows, forest edges, and anywhere there's decaying plant matter to feed on.

seasonality.spring: Most active as temperatures warm and moisture increases. Look for them emerging from winter hiding spots under logs and debris, often seen on garden plants in early morning.
seasonality.summer: Active at night and during rainy periods. Hide during hot, dry days under mulch, stones, or in soil cracks. Peak feeding time on crops and garden plants.
seasonality.fall: Continue feeding heavily to prepare for winter. Often more visible during the day as temperatures cool and moisture returns with autumn rains.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive, hiding deep in soil, under logs, or in compost piles. May emerge briefly during warm spells but generally remain dormant until spring.

funFact: Milky slugs are hermaphrodites, meaning each individual has both male and female reproductive organs, but they still need to mate with another slug to reproduce - and they can actually fire 'love darts' of calcium carbonate at potential mates during courtship!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small garden slugs, but the milky white mucus when disturbed is the dead giveaway. Remember: 'Milky slug, milky slime' - if you gently touch it and get thick white mucus on your finger instead of clear slime, you've found your milky slug.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'garden slug,' this species is actually native to Europe and was accidentally introduced to North America. It's now one of the most widespread slug species in New England and is considered a significant agricultural pest, causing millions of dollars in crop damage annually.
compareHints: The milky slug is smaller than the meadow slug and produces much more noticeable white mucus when disturbed. The chestnut slug is typically more reddish-brown in color and larger overall. Both relatives produce clearer, less milky slime, making the milky slug's defensive secretion its most reliable distinguishing feature among the smooth land slugs.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relatives, the Meadow Slug is distinguished by its completely smooth skin and preference for open habitats.

Compared to its relatives in New England, the Chestnut Slug is distinguished by its warm brown coloration - the Milky Slug tends to be grayer and produces more obvious white mucus, while the Meadow Slug is typically smaller and paler.
